proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(I_{ia}=\mathbf 1(Z_i=a)\).  By \(\texttt{ass:balanced-complete-randomization}\), for distinct units \(i\ne j\),
\[
 \mathbb E_Z I_{ia}=\frac nN,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_Z(I_{ia}I_{ja})=\frac{n(n-1)}{N(N-1)},
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_Z(I_{ia}I_{jb})=\frac{n^2}{N(N-1)}\quad(a\ne b),
\]
whereas \(I_{ia}I_{ib}=0\) when \(a\ne b\).  Define the fixed centered outcomes
\(\widetilde Y_i(a)=Y_i(a)-\bar Y(a)\).  Then
\(\sum_i\widetilde Y_i(a)=0\), and subtracting the fixed mean does not change any assignment covariance.  The preceding inclusion probabilities, together with
\(\sum_{i\ne j}\widetilde Y_i(a)\widetilde Y_j(b)=-\sum_i\widetilde Y_i(a)\widetilde Y_i(b)\), give
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_Z\{\widehat{\bar Y}(a)\mid Y\}
 =\left(\frac1n-\frac1N\right)S_{aa}(Y)
\]
and, for \(a\ne b\),
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_Z\{\widehat{\bar Y}(a),\widehat{\bar Y}(b)\mid Y\}
 =-\frac1N S_{ab}(Y).
\]
For example, the latter equality follows equation by equation from
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}_Z\{\widehat{\bar Y}(a),\widehat{\bar Y}(b)\mid Y\}
 &=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{Cov}_Z(I_{ia},I_{jb})
       \widetilde Y_i(a)\widetilde Y_j(b)\\
 &=-\frac1{N^2}\sum_i\widetilde Y_i(a)\widetilde Y_i(b)
   +\frac1{N^2(N-1)}\sum_{i\ne j}\widetilde Y_i(a)\widetilde Y_j(b)\\
 &=-\frac1{N(N-1)}\sum_i\widetilde Y_i(a)\widetilde Y_i(b)
 =-\frac1N S_{ab}(Y).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus the covariance matrix of \(\widehat{\bar Y}\) is
\(\operatorname{diag}(S_{aa}/n)-S/N\).  Applying the fixed linear map \(C\), as in \(\texttt{def:contrast-risk}\), proves
\[
 \Sigma_C(Y)=C\left\{\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{S_{aa}(Y)}n\right)_{a\in\mathcal A}-\frac{S(Y)}N\right\}C^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Finally, cyclicity of trace and \(H=C^{\mathsf T}WC\) yield
\[
 \rho_W(Y)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H\left\{\operatorname{diag}(S_{aa}/n)-S/N\right\}\right]
 =\sum_a\frac{H_{aa}S_{aa}(Y)}n-\frac1N\sum_{a,b}H_{ab}S_{ab}(Y).
\]
Holding every armwise empirical multiset fixed holds its mean and its finite-population variance \(S_{aa}(Y)\) fixed by their displayed formulas.  Therefore only the off-diagonal covariances can vary across completions.

First note that \(H\succeq0\) because \(W\succeq0\), and
\(H\mathbf 1_K=C^{\mathsf T}WC\mathbf 1_K=0\) by \(\texttt{ass:causal-contrast}\).  Consequently, in view of \(\texttt{def:rank-cone}\), the only additional requirement for \(H\in\mathcal R_K\) is \(H_{ab}\leq0\) for all \(a\ne b\).

We first prove the needed finite rearrangement fact directly.  Let
\(u_1\leq\cdots\leq u_N\) and \(v_1\leq\cdots\leq v_N\).  If a permutation \(q\) has an inversion at positions \(i<j\), so that \(v_{q(i)}>v_{q(j)}\), swapping those two assigned values changes the sum \(\sum_k u_kv_{q(k)}\) by
\[
 (u_j-u_i)\{v_{q(i)}-v_{q(j)}\}\geq0.
\]
Successively removing inversions therefore proves
\[
 \sum_i u_i v_i\geq\sum_i u_i v_{q(i)}.
\]
Subtracting the fixed product \(N\bar u\bar v\) and dividing by \(N-1>0\) shows that, among all pairings of two fixed empirical marginals, their finite-population covariance is maximized by their common increasing ranks.

Suppose now that \(H\in\mathcal R_K\).  By \(\texttt{def:completion-class}\), every column of a feasible \(Y\) is a permutation of its ordered marginal column in \(Y^{\uparrow}(F)\).  The rearrangement calculation therefore gives, simultaneously for every pair \(a<b\),
\[
 S_{ab}\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}\geq S_{ab}(Y).
\]
The diagonal terms in \(\texttt{lem:complete-randomization-risk}\) are fixed by the marginals, while symmetry of \(H\) and \(S\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \rho_W\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}-\rho_W(Y)
 &=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{a<b}(-H_{ab})
 \left[S_{ab}\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}-S_{ab}(Y)\right]\\
 &\geq0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
This proves sufficiency and the stated regret identity.

Conversely, suppose \(H_{ab}>0\) for some \(a<b\).  Let \(N\) be any multiple of \(2K\), let the marginals in arms \(a,b\) each have \(N/2\) zeros and \(N/2\) ones, and let all other arm marginals be point masses at zero.  Write \(u\) for the ordered binary column.  Common ranking pairs \(u\) with itself, whereas the feasible competing completion pairs arm \(a\)'s column \(u\) with arm \(b\)'s column \(\mathbf 1_N-u\).  The two relevant covariances are
\[
 S_{ab}\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}=\frac{N}{4(N-1)},
 \qquad
 S_{ab}(Y)=-\frac{N}{4(N-1)}.
\]
All marginal variances and all other cross-arm covariances agree between the two schedules.  Hence the already proved identity gives
\[
 \rho_W\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}-\rho_W(Y)
 =\frac2N(-H_{ab})\frac{N}{2(N-1)}
 =-\frac{H_{ab}}{N-1}<0.
\]
Thus universal common-rank optimality fails whenever an off-diagonal entry of \(H\) is positive.  Together with the automatic positive semidefiniteness and zero row sums established in the first paragraph, this proves necessity and the equivalence.

For a fixed completion pair, a symmetric matrix difference is positive semidefinite exactly when all its quadratic forms are nonnegative.  Thus the asserted universal Loewner dominance is equivalent to
\[
 h^{\mathsf T}\!left[\Sigma_C\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}-\Sigma_C(Y)\right]h\geq0
 \quad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R^m,F,Y.
\]
For a given \(h\), put \(c=C^{\mathsf T}h\).  The displayed quadratic form is the scalarized covariance difference for the one-row contrast \(c^{\mathsf T}\) and scalar weight one.  Since \(c^{\mathsf T}\mathbf 1_K=h^{\mathsf T}C\mathbf 1_K=0\), \(\texttt{thm:rank-cone-iff}\) applies and says that this scalar inequality holds universally exactly when
\[
 cc^{\mathsf T}\in\mathcal R_K,
 \quad\text{equivalently}\quad
 c_ac_b\leq0\quad(a\ne b).
\]
Therefore universal Loewner dominance is equivalent to the following property of the linear space \(L=\operatorname{range}(C^{\mathsf T})\): every \(c\in L\) has pairwise nonpositive distinct-coordinate products.

We now characterize such a space.  Every nonzero \(c\in L\) has coordinate sum zero.  It therefore has a positive and a negative coordinate.  Pairwise nonpositive products prohibit two positive coordinates and also prohibit two negative coordinates.  Hence every nonzero \(c\in L\) has exactly two nonzero coordinates and is of the form \(t(e_p-e_q)\).  Fix one such vector.  If another vector in \(L\) used a different coordinate pair, then a generic nonzero linear combination of the two vectors (choose the scalar outside the finitely many values causing coordinate cancellation) would have at least three nonzero coordinates, contradicting the preceding conclusion.  It follows that
\[
 L\subseteq\operatorname{span}(e_p-e_q)
\]
for one fixed pair \(p\ne q\).  Equivalently, all columns of \(C\) except columns \(p,q\) vanish and \(C_{\cdot q}=-C_{\cdot p}\).  Because \(C\ne0\), this is a nonzero vector rescaling of the pairwise contrast.  Conversely, this column form makes every \(C^{\mathsf T}h\) a multiple of \(e_p-e_q\), so every matrix \(cc^{\mathsf T}\) lies in \(\mathcal R_K\), proving Loewner dominance.

If \(C\) does not have this form, the characterization supplies an \(h\) and distinct arms \(a,b\) with \(c_ac_b>0\).  The binary construction in the necessity part of \(\texttt{thm:rank-cone-iff}\), applied to \(cc^{\mathsf T}\), then gives
\[
 h^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_C\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}h
 <h^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_C(Y)h.
\]
This is precisely the claimed binary witness that common ranking reduces the randomization variance in direction \(h\).

Under the stated values,
\[
 H=C^{\mathsf T}WC=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathcal R_2.
\]
Hence \(\texttt{thm:rank-cone-iff}\) proves that common ranks maximize \(\rho_W\).  Under the stated scalar choices, \(\rho_W(Y)\) is exactly
\(\operatorname{Var}_Z\{\widehat{\bar Y}(2)-\widehat{\bar Y}(1)\mid Y\}\).  The maximum is sharp because \(Y^{\uparrow}(F)\) belongs to the completion class and attains it, and it is comonotone because it pairs the two marginal order-statistic columns in their common increasing order.  This is exactly the two-arm endpoint named in the proposition.

With \(W=I_{K-1}\), one has \(H=C^{\mathsf T}C\).  Because the rows of \(C\) are an orthonormal basis of \(\mathbf 1_K^{\perp}\), \(C^{\mathsf T}C\) is the orthogonal projector onto that space.  The projector is
\[
 H=I_K-\frac1K\mathbf 1_K\mathbf 1_K^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Consequently \(H_{aa}=1-K^{-1}\), \(H_{ab}=-K^{-1}\) for \(a\ne b\), \(H\succeq0\), and \(H\mathbf 1_K=0\).  By \(\texttt{def:rank-cone}\), \(H\in\mathcal R_K\), so \(\texttt{thm:rank-cone-iff}\) proves that common ranks maximize the sum of the component randomization variances.  If \(K>2\), this \(C\) has rank \(K-1>1\), whereas a matrix supported on two opposite columns has rank at most one.  The characterization in \(\texttt{thm:loewner-boundary}\) therefore rules out universal Loewner dominance, as claimed.

Direct multiplication gives
\[
 C^{\mathsf T}C=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}=H.
\]
This matrix is positive semidefinite as a Gram matrix, has zero row sums, and has nonpositive off-diagonal entries; hence \(H\in\mathcal R_3\) by \(\texttt{def:rank-cone}\).  For the common binary column, the mean is \(1/2\) and
\[
 \frac1{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(Y_i-1/2)^2
 =\frac15\cdot6\cdot\frac14=\frac3{10}.
\]
Thus every entry of the common-rank covariance matrix is \(3/10\).  In the competing schedule, the second centered column is the negative of the first and third centered columns, proving
\(S_{12}=S_{23}=-3/10\) and \(S_{13}=3/10\).

For the common schedule, \(\sum_{a,b}H_{ab}S_{ab}=(3/10)\mathbf 1_3^{\mathsf T}H\mathbf 1_3=0\), while
\(\sum_a H_{aa}S_{aa}/n=(1+2+1)(3/10)/2=3/5\).  Therefore \(\texttt{lem:complete-randomization-risk}\) gives \(\rho_W=3/5\).  For the competing schedule,
\[
 \sum_{a,b}H_{ab}S_{ab}
 =\frac65+2\left\{(-1)\left(-\frac3{10}\right)+(-1)\left(-\frac3{10}\right)\right\}
 =\frac{12}{5},
\]
so its risk is \(3/5-(1/6)(12/5)=1/5\).  Finally the regret identity in \(\texttt{thm:rank-cone-iff}\) yields
\[
 \frac13\left\{\frac3{10}-\left(-\frac3{10}\right)+\frac3{10}-\left(-\frac3{10}\right)\right\}=\frac25,
\]
which also equals \(3/5-1/5\).

The stated matrix is the outer product
\[
 H=(1,1,-2)^{\mathsf T}(1,1,-2)
 =\begin{pmatrix}1&1&-2\\1&1&-2\\-2&-2&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It is positive semidefinite and has zero row sums, but \(H_{12}=1>0\), so \(H\notin\mathcal R_3\) by \(\texttt{def:rank-cone}\).  Each nonconstant binary column has mean \(1/2\) and variance \((5^{-1})6(1/4)=3/10\); the third column is constant.  Under common ranking, \(S_{12}=3/10\).  Thus \(\texttt{lem:complete-randomization-risk}\) gives
\[
 \rho_W\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}
 =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac3{10}+\frac3{10}\right)
 -\frac16\left\{\frac3{10}+\frac3{10}+2\frac3{10}\right\}
 =\frac1{10}.
\]
After reversing only the second column, its centered values are the negatives of those in the first, so \(S_{12}=-3/10\).  The same formula then gives
\[
 \rho_W(Y)
 =\frac3{10}-\frac16\left\{\frac3{10}+\frac3{10}-2\frac3{10}\right\}
 =\frac3{10}.
\]
Equivalently, the exact regret identity gives
\[
 \rho_W\{Y^{\uparrow}(F)\}-\rho_W(Y)
 =\frac13(-1)\left\{\frac3{10}-\left(-\frac3{10}\right)\right\}
 =-\frac15.
\]
The reversed schedule preserves both nondegenerate empirical marginals and the degenerate third marginal, so it is a valid member of \(\mathcal S_6(F)\) and is the required strict finite witness.

theorem.statement:
Fix \(\Omega\in\mathfrak K^{\mathrm{bal}}_{N,K}\) and let \(E=\mathcal A\times\{1,\ldots,N-1\}\).  For \(\pi\in\mathfrak S_N\) and \(\sigma\in\mathfrak S_N^K\), define the symmetric \(|E|\times|E|\) matrix \(B^{\pi,\sigma}\), indexed by \((a,r),(b,s)\in E\), by
\[
 B^{\pi,\sigma}_{(a,r),(b,s)}
 =H_{ab}\sum_{i,j=1}^N\Omega_{ab,\pi(i),\pi(j)}
 \left[(d_r)_i(d_s)_j-(d_r)_{\sigma_a(i)}(d_s)_{\sigma_b(j)}\right].
\]
Then
\[
 [\Omega]_{\cong}\in\mathfrak C^{\mathrm{bal}}_{N,K}(H)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{there is a \(\pi\in\mathfrak S_N\) such that every \(B^{\pi,\sigma}\) is copositive},
\]
where copositive means \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}B^{\pi,\sigma}\alpha\geq0\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R_+^{K(N-1)}\).  This gives an exact finite recognition algorithm: enumerate \(\pi\) and \(\sigma\), and test copositivity by enumerating principal supports.  If \(H\) and \(\Omega\) are rational, every test is an exact real-algebraic sign test.  A yes instance returns a relabelling and the finite support-spectral certificates.  A no instance returns, for every common relabelling \(\pi\), an arm-specific permutation \(\sigma\) and rational nonnegative cut increments \(\alpha\) for which the loss improvement is strict.

For a no instance, define
\[
 L^*(H,\Omega)=
 \max_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_N}
 \min_{\substack{\sigma\in\mathfrak S_N^K,\ \alpha\geq0\\
 \alpha^{\mathsf T}B^{\pi,\sigma}\alpha<0}}
 \max_{a\in\mathcal A}\left(1+\#\{r:\alpha_{(a,r)}>0\}\right).
\]
Then \(L^*(H,\Omega)\) is exactly the smallest per-arm alphabet size sufficient for a complete family of strict witnesses against all common relabellings.  In particular \(L^*(H,\Omega)\leq N\), and binary witnesses are complete for the given no instance exactly when \(L^*(H,\Omega)\leq2\).  The exhaustive algorithm is finite but generally exponential in \(N\) and \(K\); this partial resolution does not establish the polynomial running-time requested in the question.
theorem.proof_tex:
Fix \(\pi\) and abbreviate \(\widetilde\Omega=\Omega^\pi\).  By \(\texttt{def:admissible-balanced-kernel}\),
\[
 \sum_i\widetilde\Omega_{abij}=0
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \sum_j\widetilde\Omega_{abij}=0
\]
for every \(a,b,i,j\) of the remaining type.  Every ordered column has the unique adjacent-increment expansion from \(\texttt{def:kernel-cut-handle}\),
\[
 x^a=x^a_1\mathbf 1_N+\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}\alpha_{(a,r)}d_r,
 \qquad
 \alpha_{(a,r)}=x^a_{r+1}-x^a_r\geq0.
\]
The two unit-sum identities annihilate every term involving a constant column.  Substitution into \(\texttt{def:balanced-kernel-loss}\) therefore gives the exact identity
\[
 N^2\left\{\mathscr L_{H,\Omega^\pi}(x,\mathrm{id})-
 \mathscr L_{H,\Omega^\pi}(x,\sigma)\right\}
 =\alpha^{\mathsf T}B^{\pi,\sigma}\alpha.
\]
The covariance symmetry \(\Omega_{abij}=\Omega_{baji}\) and symmetry of \(H\) show, after interchanging \((a,r,i)\) with \((b,s,j)\), that \(B^{\pi,\sigma}\) is symmetric.  Since every \(\alpha\geq0\) produces ordered columns through the displayed expansion, and every ordered column produces such an \(\alpha\), the identity proves
\[
 \Omega^\pi\in\mathcal C_{N,K}(H)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 B^{\pi,\sigma}\text{ is copositive for every }\sigma.
\]
Taking the existential quantifier over \(\pi\) and applying \(\texttt{def:admissible-rank-kernel-domain}\) proves the first asserted equivalence.

It remains to justify that the test and certificates are finite.  For any real symmetric \(q\times q\) matrix \(B\), the following elementary support criterion holds:
\[
 B\text{ is not copositive}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{some nonempty principal submatrix \(B_{TT}\) has a negative eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector}.
\]
The reverse implication is immediate by extending the positive eigenvector by zeros.  For the forward implication, minimize \(v^{\mathsf T}Bv\) on the compact set \(\{v\geq0:\|v\|_2=1\}\).  If \(B\) is not copositive, the minimum \(\lambda\) is negative.  On the support \(T\) of a minimizer, all coordinates are strictly positive, so the Lagrange multiplier equation in the relative interior of that coordinate face is
\(B_{TT}v_T=\lambda v_T\).  This proves the criterion.  There are only \(2^q-1\) nonempty supports.  Combined with the finite sets \(\mathfrak S_N\) and \(\mathfrak S_N^K\), it yields the asserted terminating enumeration.  With rational input, characteristic-polynomial root isolation and exact sign determination in the associated algebraic eigenspaces decide every support condition.  On a failing support, strict negativity is open, so a sufficiently close rational positive vector retains \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}B\alpha<0\); exact interval refinement constructs one.

For such a rational vector, set
\[
 x^a=\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}\alpha_{(a,r)}d_r.
\]
The loss identity proves that \(\sigma\) strictly improves on identity.  This arm column has exactly one plus the number of its positive adjacent increments as an upper bound on its number of distinct values, and, after deleting zero increments, that count is exact.  Minimizing this discrete count over all strict witnesses for a fixed \(\pi\), and then taking the maximum over the relabellings that all must be refuted, proves the formula for \(L^*(H,\Omega)\).  Each arm has at most \(N-1\) positive increments, so \(L^*(H,\Omega)\leq N\); the value is at most two exactly when one cut per nonconstant arm suffices.  The displayed enumeration has factorial and exponential components, so it proves exact decidability and certificate production, but not a polynomial running-time bound.
